newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Starbucks casts wider Asian net.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Starbucks casts wider Asian net.

text.p: U.S. coffee shop operator Starbucks Corp is optimistic about transferring Seattle's "social beverage" and quaint cafe culture to Asia, chairman and chief executive officer Howard Schultz said on Friday.
"I really believe there is an opportunity for us to have more stores in the Pacific rim than we have in North America," Schultz told Reuters in an interview.
He did not specify a timeframe when Asia might overtake the U.S. in outlets but predicted "strong" opportunities to transfer the passion for coffee to Asia.
Schultz attributed the higher growth in coffee consumption to a change in social habits, where people need a "third place" away from home and office to seek respite.
"One of the most surprising statistics, when you look at worldwide consumption of coffee, is that the fastest areas of coffee consumption are in the Pacific rim," Schultz said.
Schultz, in Singapore to open Starbucks' second store in a trendy downtown shopping centre, noted the company's target of 200 stores in Asia by the year 2000 was well within reach.
Starbucks, which has about 1,102 stores in North America, has three in Japan and launched its first Singapore outfit, also the first in Southeast Asia, in December.
He said Starbucks is likely be ready to announce plans to open stores in other Asian markets by the end of the year.
Commenting on the company's performance over the Christmas period and the first fiscal quarter ending December 29 he said: "I think sales were quite good for the first quarter."
He said for the end of fiscal 1996 (ending in September) the company's gross sales totalled approximately $700 million, the ninth consecutive year where sales grew 50 percent or more.

A major part of the company's commitment to the Asia Pacific are plans to build a roasting plant here before the end of the decade, and an analysis is currently being conducted to study issues like distribution and economies of sale, Schultz said.
He did not specify where the plant might be located, but said it would be decided by year-end.
"We are making a very deep commitment to this market and we believe strongly that we'll have significant presence throughout Asia, especially in Singapore....," he said.
Asked about Starbucks' plans in Europe, Schultz said: "We'll enter Europe before the end of the decade, but the opportunity for Starbucks in Asia is more attractive right now."

Starbucks invested about US$10 million in developing its Asian operations at the end of last year, which rises to about $20 million if contributions of joint venture partners in the region are taken into account.
Schultz dismissed speculation about the impact of coffee prices, up a sharp 50 percent over the past two months, on the company's retail operations.
March arabica coffee futures in New York hit U.S. 180.05 cents a pound on Thursday, their highest levels in 21 months.

Asked about hedging on futures markets, Schultz said: "We have not gotten into that business, we have just viewed that as a discipline. We're a coffee company, a retailer, we're not commodity buyers. You have to know what you do well and do it."
For the fiscal first quarter ending December 29, the Seattle-based coffee chain reported net income of US$14.4 million, compared with $9.6 million, in the same period a year-earlier.
"There's been very little impact for us. Most of our needs for coffee in fiscal 1997 (ending September 30) have been purchased," Schultz said.
He said that despite other companies having raised coffee prices in line with volatility in futures markets, Starbucks had no plans to hike prices in the near-term.
"I hope we won't have to do that...irregardless of the price we have to pay for coffee, we will only pursue the top quality coffee in the world as we have in the last 25 years," he said.
Coffee prices have risen sharply due to low U.S. stocks and tight supplies in the main growing countries of South America.
